source.spoken_script: From the cross, in His darkest hour, Jesus reached for words already written — a psalm David had penned a thousand years before. Psalm twenty-two opens in the voice of a forsaken man; Jesus made it His own. David's very first line: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" A thousand years later, at the ninth hour, Jesus cried it from the cross: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" The very same words. This was no cry of lost faith — even forsaken, He still calls God "my God." It was the sinless Son taking our place, and bearing the forsaking that our sin deserved. He was forsaken so that you never will be. However far you've run, the way home is open — and He opened it from the dark.

He was forsaken so that you never will be. However far you have run, the way home is open, and he opened it from the dark.

platforms.label: YouTube (Long-form 16:9)
platforms.title: The Forsaken Cry: Why Jesus Quoted Psalm 22 From the Cross
platforms.description:
At the ninth hour, from the darkness over Golgotha (Psalm 22:1, Matthew 27:46), Jesus cried out with a loud voice. And the words he chose were not new. They were a thousand years old.

"My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?" (Psalm 22:1, KJV).

David's psalm opens in the voice of a forsaken man, and Jesus made that voice his own, quoting the very first line as his own cry.

But hear what the cry is not. It is not lost faith. Even forsaken, he still says MY God, twice. The possessive survives the dark. This is the sinless Son standing in our place, bearing the forsaking that our sin deserved, so that the door home would stand open from the inside of the darkness itself.

In this piece: the ninth-hour darkness, David's opening line and why Jesus reached for it, what the cry does and does not mean, and the exchange at its center: he was forsaken so that you never will be.

However far you have run, the way home is open. He opened it from the dark.
